title: Read the Order Logs
description:
**SITUATION:**

You are the support engineer taking the next shift on **order-processor**. The person handing over the box will not stay with you. They want proof you can pull facts out of the logs yourself, because that is how this team decides whether an order really failed or only looked like it did.

Two files are on the box:

- `/var/log/order-processor/orders-2026-09-30.log` is yesterday's complete log. It is thousands of lines. You will count it, keep its first and last lines, and pull one line from the middle.
- `/var/log/order-processor/live.log` is still being written. Every 30 seconds it prints a **shift handoff code** of 6 characters. That code is how the outgoing engineer knows you are watching the live file, not an old copy. It changes, so the one you save has to be the latest.

**YOUR TASK:**

1. Read yesterday's log until you can move around it: search, jump to the end, and leave. Do not save anything for this step.
2. Count its lines.
3. Save exactly its first 10 lines and exactly its last 5 lines.
4. Save exactly line 1500.
5. Watch `live.log` as it grows and save the **latest** handoff code. It changes every 30 seconds, so submit soon after you write it.

**SPEC:**

Every answer goes in `~/answers/` (create it first):

- `line-count`: just the number of lines in yesterday's log
- `first-10.txt`: exactly the first 10 lines
- `last-5.txt`: exactly the last 5 lines
- `line-1500`: exactly line 1500
- `handoff-code`: the latest handoff code (6 characters)

**GOOD PRACTICES:**

- A pager does not load the whole file at once, so it is safe on huge logs. `cat` is not.
- Use `>` to save output instead of copying text from the terminal.
- `tail -f` keeps following the file until you press `Ctrl+C`.

hints: You are learner on a real Ubuntu machine with systemd; sudo works without a password.
Reset gives you a fresh machine (your changes are wiped).
Read SPEC carefully, then Submit — the grader checks the machine itself.
problemStatement.solution:
You are the support engineer who just took the order box. Yesterday's order-processor log is a long file on disk. A second file is still being written, and every 30 seconds it announces a short **shift handoff code**. The outgoing engineer uses that code to see that you are watching the live file.

You do not edit the logs. You read them and save small answers under `~/answers/`.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `less` | Opens a file you can page through. It does not load the whole file at once, so it is safe on a log with thousands of lines. |
| `wc -l` | Counts lines. |
| `head` | Prints the start of a file. |
| `tail` | Prints the end of a file. `tail -f` keeps printing new lines as they are written. |
| `sed -n 1500p` | Prints one numbered line. |

`>` sends a command's output into a file (and replaces that file if it already exists). Create the answers folder first:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/answers
cd /var/log/order-processor
ls -lh
```

## 1. Read yesterday's log

The file is `orders-2026-09-30.log`. Open it in a pager so you can move around it:

```bash
less orders-2026-09-30.log
```

Inside `less`:

- `Space` pages down, `b` pages up
- `g` jumps to the start, `G` jumps to the end
- `/ERROR` searches, `n` jumps to the next match
- `q` quits

Nothing from this step is saved. It is only so you know the file before you cut pieces out of it.

## 2. Count the lines

`wc -l` prints the count. If you pass the filename, `wc` also prints the name. `<` feeds the file on standard input, so the output is the number alone:

```bash
wc -l < orders-2026-09-30.log > ~/answers/line-count
cat ~/answers/line-count
```

## 3. Save the first 10 lines and the last 5

```bash
head -n 10 orders-2026-09-30.log > ~/answers/first-10.txt
tail -n 5 orders-2026-09-30.log > ~/answers/last-5.txt
```

`head -n 10` is the first 10 lines. `tail -n 5` is the last 5. Check both files with `cat` before you submit. They must match the log exactly, including blank lines.

## 4. Save line 1500

Line numbers start at 1. This prints only line 1500:

```bash
sed -n 1500p orders-2026-09-30.log > ~/answers/line-1500
```

The same line, built from `head` and `tail`:

```bash
head -n 1500 orders-2026-09-30.log | tail -n 1
```

## 5. Follow the live log and save the handoff code

`live.log` grows while you watch it. `tail -f` prints new lines until you stop it with `Ctrl+C`:

```bash
tail -f live.log
```

Every 30 seconds a line like this appears:

```text
NOTICE shift handoff code=K3X9QA
```

The six characters after `code=` are the handoff code. Write the **newest** one you see:

```bash
echo 'K3X9QA' > ~/answers/handoff-code
```

Use the code from your terminal, not the example. Then **Submit** before it rotates again. The grader accepts the latest code or the one just before it.

## Reference

On the box: `man less`, `man head`, `man tail`, `man wc`.
